title: "10 for $10" Doesn't Mean You Buy 10
editorialNotes: The "10 for $10 rings up at $1 each" claim is sourced to FTC consumer guidance in the Notion source index; kept as body copy, never hero type.

copy.headline: "10 for $10" does not mean you have to buy 10.
Most "10 for $10" deals ring up at $1 each no matter how many you grab.
items: The store formats it as a bulk number because your brain reads it as a bundle.
You feel pressure to hit the number.

copy.headline: Same trick, different label: "3 for $9" yogurts.
items: You don't need 3. You just think you do because the sign grouped them.

copy.headline: End-cap displays use the same psychology.
copy.body: The product isn't on sale — it's on a paid advertising spot. Brands pay thousands for end-cap placement. That "deal" is a media buy, not a discount.

copy.headline: BOGO (Buy One Get One) is the most effective version.
items: The second one expires before you use it.
copy.body: Net cost: higher than buying one at full price.

copy.headline: The rule: check the unit price tag on the shelf (small print, bottom left).
items: It shows cost per ounce or per count.
That number is the only number that matters.

copy.headline: Grocery stores are designed to make you overbuy. Every extra item you don't eat is money in the trash.
copy.ctaLine: fond tracks what you actually use — so you buy what you need. Link in bio.
